To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) The optimal localisation of biofuels in Europe is dependent on the policy instrument used to promote biofuels.

biofuel production in the EU is optimal when it is located in regions where biomass is available at a low cost and when it is combined with heat and/or electricity production, and that the optimal biofuel share is highly sensitive to the fossil fuel price and to the CO2 emission mitigation policy.
biofuel support and CO2 cost have a large effect on bioenergy production and that the use of biofuels is not necessarily a cost-effective way to reduce CO2 emissions.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development and use, for analysis of bioenergy production scenarios, of an optimisation tool suitable for analysis of second generation biofuel and bioelectricity production on a European-wide scale.
the optimal localisation of second generation biofuel use in Europe and its implications for bioenergy use in the EU.
the optimal use of biomass for bioenergy production.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a large-scale biofuel expansion is not a viable option for CO2 emission mitigation in the EU.
biofuels are not necessarily a good solution to climate change, but that they may be a good solution to the EU’s bioenergy policy.
a large-scale production of biofuels is not a certain way towards a low carbon economy, and that the biofuels production potential is not unlimited.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
biofuel production in the EU can be increased substantially with a combination of targeted support and a CO-2 cost of around EUR 60/t CO2.
the use of biofuels in the EU transport sector can be cost-effective, but the costs depend heavily on the assumptions regarding biofuel feedstock availability.
the optimal biofuel production is a function of the price of fossil fuels and the cost of CO2.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the EU biofuel target of 10% of total transport fuel demand by 2020 is not a given.
bioenergy can be a valuable part of the EU energy system, but only if it is optimally used.
bioenergy is a promising technology, which has the potential to make a significant contribution to CO2 emission mitigation in the transport sector.
